note: This was largely a war without front lines. Areas show provinces on the dates their main towns changed hands (2001 and 2021) and a few well-documented Taliban strongholds in between; the countryside was often contested and is not mapped.

chapters.title: The 2001 campaign: Kabul and Kandahar fall
arrows: Dostum and Atta advance on Mazar-i-Sharif
Daud's forces take Taloqan and Kunduz
chapters.text: After the 11 September attacks, the United States and Britain began bombing the Taliban on 7 October 2001, while CIA teams and US Special Forces worked with the Northern Alliance. Mazar-i-Sharif fell on 9–10 November, the Taliban abandoned Kabul on 13 November and within a day the provinces on the Iranian border had changed hands; Kunduz, their last city in the north, fell on 25 November. Kandahar, the Taliban heartland, was surrendered on 7 December. Provinces are coloured when their main town changed hands; who held the countryside was often unclear.

chapters.title: Tora Bora
chapters.text: Al-Qaeda and Taliban fighters, possibly including Osama bin Laden, gathered in bunkers and caves at Tora Bora in the Spin Ghar mountains south-west of Jalalabad. The US bombed the area from 16 November, and Afghan militias advised by American and British special forces attacked from early December. The complex fell by 17 December, but bin Laden had escaped, probably into Pakistan.

chapters.title: The Taliban return in the south
arrows: Afghan and coalition forces retake Musa Qala
chapters.text: By 2006 the Taliban insurgency had returned in force to the south, where British troops now held Helmand and Canadians Kandahar. In Operation Medusa (2–17 September 2006) Canadian-led NATO forces drove the Taliban out of their stronghold around Pashmul, west of Kandahar. The Taliban overran the town of Musa Qala in February 2007 and held it until Afghan, British and US forces retook it on 7–12 December. Elsewhere control of the countryside was contested and changed often, so only these strongholds are mapped.

chapters.title: The surge in Helmand and Kandahar
chapters.text: In summer 2009 British troops (Operation Panther's Claw) and US Marines (Operation Khanjar) pushed into Taliban-held districts along the Helmand river, and in December President Obama ordered 30,000 more US troops to Afghanistan. In February 2010 Operation Moshtarak took Marjah, the largest Taliban-held town in Helmand; the Afghan flag was formally raised there on 25 February. From September 2010 Operation Dragon Strike cleared the districts west of Kandahar city. The extra US troops left in 2011–12.

chapters.title: Kunduz, 2015
chapters.text: NATO's combat mission ended in December 2014, leaving Afghan forces to fight with foreign training, air support and special forces. Taliban fighters pressed on Kunduz from April 2015, and on 28 September they overran the city, the first provincial capital they had taken since 2001, while government troops fell back to the airport. Afghan forces with US air and special-forces support retook the centre from 1 October, and the Taliban withdrew by 13 October. On 3 October a US air strike destroyed the Médecins Sans Frontières hospital, killing 22 people.

chapters.title: The Doha agreement and the US withdrawal
chapters.text: On 29 February 2020 the United States and the Taliban signed an agreement in Doha: US and allied troops would leave within 14 months if the Taliban kept its commitments, which included talks with the Afghan government. Those talks made little progress. The Taliban launched a major offensive on 1 May 2021 and took many rural districts, but control of the countryside shifted daily and is not mapped here. US troops left Bagram, their main base, on 2 July.

chapters.title: The Taliban take over, August 2021
chapters.text: Zaranj, in the far south-west, became the first provincial capital to fall, on 6 August 2021. In ten days almost all the others followed, often after surrenders: Kunduz on 8 August, Herat and Kandahar on 12–13 August, Mazar-i-Sharif on 14 August, and Jalalabad and Kabul on 15 August, when the Republic collapsed. The US and its partners evacuated more than 123,000 people through Kabul airport before the last US troops left on 30 August; the Panjshir valley was still holding out. Provinces are coloured on the day their capital fell.

battles.name: Fall of Mazar-i-Sharif
battles.casualties: c. 340 killed: 38 Northern Alliance and about 300 Taliban, with 250 Taliban captured

battles.name: Siege of Kunduz
battles.casualties: c. 2,000 Taliban killed or wounded; 3,000–3,500 surrendered

battles.name: Battle of Qala-i-Jangi
battles.casualties: over 570 killed, most of them Taliban prisoners

battles.name: Battle of Tora Bora
battles.casualties: c. 220 al-Qaeda and Taliban killed and 60 captured; Afghan militia losses unknown

battles.name: Operation Medusa
battles.casualties: NATO claimed 512 Taliban killed; 17 NATO and Afghan soldiers killed in the fighting, and 14 British airmen in an air crash

battles.name: Battle of Musa Qala
battles.casualties: fewer than 100 Taliban (ISAF claim) to several hundred (Afghan claim); 2 ISAF soldiers killed

battles.name: Operation Panther's Claw
battles.casualties: over 200 Taliban (British claim); 26 British and Afghan killed

battles.name: Operation Moshtarak (Marjah)
battles.casualties: 73+ coalition and Afghan soldiers, 120+ Taliban in the first five days and 28 civilians killed

battles.name: Battle of Kunduz
battles.casualties: 38 Afghan soldiers and police and 80–200 Taliban killed (government figures); 848+ civilians killed or wounded

battles.name: Battle of Kandahar (2021)
battles.casualties: 100+ civilians killed or wounded; military losses unknown
